records.sourceFile: Mental Fatigue Impairs Endurance Performance- A Physiological Explanation.pdf

paper.citation: Martin K, Meeusen R, Thompson KG, Keegan R, Rattray B. Mental Fatigue Impairs Endurance Performance: A Physiological Explanation. Sports Medicine. 2018.
paper.abstract: This theoretical review proposes that extracellular cerebral adenosine accumulates during demanding cognitive work and increases perceived exertion and reduces motivation during later endurance exercise. The authors review evidence to support and extend this hypothesis, noting that heart rate, lactate and neuromuscular function are generally unaffected by mental fatigue.
paper.tldr: Mental fatigue appears to impair endurance mainly by raising perceived exertion, and the authors propose that adenosine built up during demanding cognitive work is the cause. This remains a hypothesis that has not been tested directly in humans.
paper.methods: Theoretical narrative review. It draws on animal pharmacology, human caffeine and sleep deprivation studies, and brain imaging work. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: The review states that mental fatigue impairs endurance performance and that heart rate, lactate and neuromuscular function are generally unaffected. It proposes that adenosine acting in the anterior cingulate cortex raises perceived exertion and impairs motivation through an interaction with dopamine. The authors note that adenosine has not been directly evaluated for effects on perceived exertion during exercise in humans.
paper.limitations: The authors acknowledge that adenosine is probably one of several contributors and that direct measurement of adenosine in humans is not currently possible. The review contains no new data, and its mechanism depends on animal and indirect pharmacological evidence.
paper.practicalImplications: The review suggests that reducing adenosine build-up during mental exertion might lessen the effect of mental fatigue on endurance, but this has not been tested. The authors note that self-report is the only available measure of motivation and is prone to social desirability bias, so motivation ratings should be read with caution.
paper.athleteDev: The review suggests that mentally fatigued athletes may fail endurance efforts through higher perceived exertion, while heart rate and lactate are not affected. The adenosine mechanism remains a hypothesis and should not yet change training or competition plans.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Mental Fatigue Negatively Impacts Cognitive and Physical Performance Outcomes - A Large-Scale Randomized Crossover Trial.pdf

paper.citation: Habay J, Arenales Arauz YL, Proost M, Schampheleer E, Lathouwers E, De Pauw K, et al. Mental Fatigue Negatively Impacts Cognitive and Physical Performance Outcomes: A Large-Scale Randomized Crossover Trial. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2026;58(2):225-241.
paper.abstract: A randomized crossover trial in 117 healthy adults compared a 45-minute Stroop task with a documentary before a GoNoGo task and a 20-minute cycling time trial. The Stroop task slowed GoNoGo reaction time and increased mental fatigue, RPE and sleepiness during the time trial, and cadence was lower after it. The time-trial distance difference was only a trend (P = 0.059).
paper.tldr: In healthy adults, 45 minutes of a Stroop task slowed a GoNoGo reaction time task and raised perceived fatigue and effort during a cycling time trial. The effect on time-trial distance was small and not statistically significant, so the physical effect is weaker than the title suggests.
paper.methods: Healthy adults aged 18 to 50 completed a familiarization visit and then two counterbalanced visits, one with a 45-minute individualized Stroop task and one with a documentary. Outcomes were GoNoGo performance, a 20-minute cycling time trial and subjective ratings, analysed with paired t tests, mixed models and non-parametric tests.
paper.findings: Go reaction time after the task was slower in the Stroop condition (380.45 vs 367.30 ms; interaction P < 0.001). Time-trial distance was 12.6 vs 12.8 km (P = 0.059, d = 0.20) and cadence was 87 vs 88 rpm (P = 0.042, d = 0.22). Power output, workload, heart rate, lactate, motivation and Go and NoGo accuracy did not differ, while mental fatigue, physical fatigue and RPE (P = 0.002) were higher during the time trial and sleepiness was higher overall in the Stroop condition.
paper.limitations: The distance and cadence effects are small and vary widely between individuals, and the authors say the 45-minute induction may not have been long enough to show the full cognitive effect. The analysed sample is unclear (117 in the baseline table versus 104 who completed all steps), and only one induction protocol in healthy adults aged 18 to 50 was tested.
paper.practicalImplications: A demanding cognitive task before a hard effort may make the effort feel harder and slightly reduce cadence, so cognitive load is worth considering before testing or hard sessions. The physical effects were small and the distance result was not statistically significant, so the study does not justify large changes to training or competition plans.
paper.athleteDev: A prolonged demanding cognitive task before exercise may raise perceived effort and reduce cadence in a cycling time trial, with only a small and non-significant effect on distance. The study used a laboratory Stroop task in healthy adults, so its effect size should be read as an estimate for this design, not a sport-specific prediction.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy adults and did not assess injured athletes or return-to-sport tasks, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Multimodal Imaging of Retired Professional Contact Sport Athletes Does Not Provide Evidence of Structural and Functional Brain Damage.pdf

paper.citation: Zivadinov R, Polak P, Schweser F, Bergsland N, Hagemeier J, Dwyer MG, et al. Multimodal Imaging of Retired Professional Contact Sport Athletes Does Not Provide Evidence of Structural and Functional Brain Damage. Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation. 2018.
paper.abstract: This 3 tesla multimodal MRI study compared 21 retired professional football and hockey players with 21 age-matched noncontact sport athletes. It found no significant group differences in white matter abnormalities, brain volumes, diffusion, susceptibility, spectroscopy or perfusion measures.
paper.tldr: In 21 retired professional football and hockey players compared with 21 noncontact athletes, a multimodal MRI battery found no significant differences in brain structure, diffusion, iron, metabolism or perfusion. The sample was too small to rule out smaller effects, so the result is not evidence that contact sport is safe for the brain.
paper.methods: Substudy of a larger project of retired athletes; 21 retired contact sport athletes and 21 age-matched noncontact athletes were scanned on a 3 tesla scanner with proton-density/T2, FLAIR, 3D T1, diffusion (tract-based spatial statistics), susceptibility (QSM and microbleeds), single-voxel spectroscopy and perfusion sequences. Group differences were tested with ANCOVA adjusted for age, body mass index and education, with Cohen's d and Cramer's V effect sizes.
paper.findings: Twelve of 21 contact athletes (57.1%) and 11 of 21 controls (52.4%) had white matter signal abnormalities, with no significant differences in lesion measures or in global and regional brain volumes. No diffusion, susceptibility, spectroscopy or perfusion measures differed significantly between groups, and microbleeds were present in 2 of 21 contact athletes (9.5%) versus 7 of 21 controls (33%; P = .067). The authors report the effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals so readers can judge the size of the differences, which were not significant.
paper.limitations: The authors state that the sample was too small to detect differences in the brain measures and refer other limitations to the companion paper. Several perfusion and susceptibility comparisons show moderate to large effect sizes (for example, accumbens mean transit time d = 0.97) and 95% confidence intervals that exclude zero while the covariate-adjusted P values are non-significant, Table 2 gives a globus pallidus mean diffusivity of 0.5 for controls against 0.87 for athletes (effect size 6.95), which looks like a reporting error, and the mild cognitive impairment subgroup comparison mentioned in the discussion is not shown.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not present this study as evidence that retired contact athletes have normal brains, because it was too small to detect moderate differences. It tested group differences, not individual diagnosis, so it gives no basis for using these MRI measures to judge an individual athlete's brain health.
paper.athleteDev: The study measures brain structure and perfusion, not performance, so it has no direct training or performance application. The paper does not report cognitive test results, so staff should not cite it as reassurance about long-term cognitive performance.
paper.rtp: The study compares retired athletes and does not examine current players or those after a head injury, so it cannot guide return to play or clearance after concussion. A normal-appearing MRI in this study does not support clearing an injured athlete.
